Before feeds and algorithms, a profile was a room you decorated yourself. Friendster and Multiply let Filipinos choose layouts, post blogs, and share photo albums with friends and relatives, including those abroad.

Friendster saw mainstream success roughly from 2005 to 2010 before Facebook took over; it shut down in 2015.

Singing has always been a Filipino pastime, once often done in the open at fiestas and street gatherings. In the 2000s, family karaoke bars offered private rooms with songbooks, screens, food, and drinks.

Celebrations moved indoors: birthdays and reunions could now be held in a room booked for the family.

Did you know Commercial KTV hubs emerged as popular enclosed leisure spaces, shifting family singing celebrations from open public streets into private rooms.

items.label: Social · 2020–2026
items.title: Everyone Became a Broadcaster
items.tpl:
Social · 2020–2026

Everyone Became a Broadcaster

TikTok and similar platforms took over from television as the engine of trends. Everyday Filipinos now film their own videos and join online movements (Kemp, 2025; Mariano, 2020).

Connect the dots: then to now

What stayed the same. The wish to belong has not changed. What has changed is who makes the content.

Filipinos no longer just watch TV stars; they pick up a smartphone, make their own videos and share them with everyone online (Mariano, 2020). Cheap texting in the 2000s had already put the phone at the center of social life (Montecillo, 2008), and the lockdowns then pushed school, work and hangouts onto screens (Malasig, 2020). The result cuts both ways: anyone can start a trend or a movement, as the community pantries showed (Philippine Daily Inquirer, 2022), yet social life now leans heavily on screens.

items.label: Economic · 2020–2026
items.title: Earning and Spending on the Phone
items.tpl:
Economic · 2020–2026

Earning and Spending on the Phone

Today Filipinos pay by QR code, shop online, and sell or perform on live streams, all while coping with rising prices (Cacho-Laurejas, 2025; Morales & dela Cruz, 2023; Newsbytes.PH, 2023).

Connect the dots: then to now

What stayed the same. People still look for income beyond a regular job. They now build it online instead of waiting in line.

Economic life shifted from risky crowds chasing cash prizes (Araneta, 2006) to live-stream storefronts paid for with mobile wallets (Cacho-Laurejas, 2025; Newsbytes.PH, 2023). BPO jobs in the 2000s had already trained Filipinos to earn from screens and foreign clients (Philippine Daily Inquirer, 2018). The trade-off: earning and paying are easier and safer, but many sellers now depend on platforms and must go live daily, while inflation squeezes budgets (Morales & dela Cruz, 2023).

items.tpl:

Politics in the Feed

Filipinos follow political vloggers, argue in comment sections, and still march when outraged (Flores, 2025; Laqui, 2025).

Connect the dots: then to now

What stayed the same. The wish to be heard remains. Influencers and algorithms now sit between people and the news.

Campaigning has moved from street rallies to social media feeds, where votes are now courted (Flores, 2025). The 2000s had already shown that pop culture could carry political messages, from ringtones to effigies (Adraneda, 2007; Bulatlat, 2008); today vloggers play that role on a far larger scale. It cuts both ways: more Filipinos can join political debates, but fake news travels faster, prompting hearings and arrest orders (Clapano, 2025).

Phones now receive emergency alerts automatically, while fans and celebrities run online donation drives (ABS-CBN News, 2024; Newman, 2018).

Connect the dots: then to now

What stayed the same. People still rely on one another. They now expect faster systems.

Emergency safety moved from waiting for news updates to receiving automatic phone warnings, which the law now requires (Free Mobile Disaster Alerts Act, 2014). Ondoy showed that ordinary Filipinos could organize rescues online (Palatino, 2009), a habit that has grown into today's rapid donation drives (ABS-CBN News, 2024). Response is faster, yet hazards like Taal still displace hundreds of thousands (Associated Press, 2020).

Personal Devices, Digital Identity

Nearly everyone now games on a personal device, registers a SIM, and follows esports stars online (Arasa, 2025; Aurelio et al., 2022; Lukman, 2026).

Connect the dots: then to now

What stayed the same. The wish to take part is unchanged. People now join as players, streamers and verified users.

The basic cellphone that once carried simple text messages has grown into a personal device that does almost everything (Arasa, 2025). Text-voting shows in the 2000s made audiences active participants (Anarcon, 2019), and today Filipino gamers perform for millions of viewers (Lukman, 2026). 86% of Filipino knowledge workers already use AI at work, above the 75% global average (Microsoft Philippines, 2024), and 78% of Filipino digital users rely on AI tools to find content and simplify tasks ("Philippine Digital Economy Surges On," 2025).

After texting and video calls, AI chat assistants will likely become the next everyday tool Filipinos use to talk, translate, and keep in touch.

TikTok already lets users turn a single photo into a moving video with its AI Alive tool, and it labels the result as AI-generated (TikTok, 2025).

Mass trends that moved from noontime TV to user-made TikTok videos will likely be co-created with AI, so anyone can join a trend, even without dancing on camera.

The DICT has set up about 19,000 free Wi-Fi sites, aims for 60,000 to 70,000 sites in 2026, and plans to use low-earth orbit satellites (Jose, 2025).

Like the comshop and the community pantry, public spaces with free internet will likely become shared social spaces where people gather online and offline at the same time.
